松原忠司.note: Historical Shinsengumi captain of the Fourth Unit, a master of the Sekiguchi school of jūjutsu; died in 1865.

吉村貫一郎.note: Historical inspector of the corps, a Nanbu (Morioka) man; later the subject of Asada Jirō's novel Mibu Gishi Den.

勝海舟.note: Katsu Kaishū (1823–1899), the far-sighted shogunal official who built the first Japanese navy and, in 1868, negotiated the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

松平慶永.note: Matsudaira Yoshinaga (Shungaku, 1828–1890), lord of Echizen Fukui, one of the leading reform-minded daimyō of the day and a voice for a union of court and shogunate.

後醍醐天皇.note: The fourteenth-century emperor whose brief Kenmu Restoration (1333) overthrew the Kamakura shogunate; Kusunoki Masashige was his most famous loyal general.

恩智左近.note: A retainer of Kusunoki Masashige, remembered as a loyal lieutenant; Kondō casts Toshizō in the part.

永井主水正尚志.note: Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official (here Grand Inspector). Mondo-no-shō is his court title. He led the 1865 embassy that interrogated Chōshū at Hiroshima.

宍戸備後助.note: A borrowed domain-elder’s name under which Chōshū sent a stand-in envoy to the Hiroshima interrogation.

山県半蔵.note: The real name of Chōshū’s sham envoy: Shishido Tamaki (1829–1901), a middle-rank samurai chosen for his glib tongue, after the Restoration a viscount and member of the House of Peers.

レオン・ロッシュ.note: Léon Roches (1809–1900), French minister to Japan 1864–68, who tied France to the shogunate’s cause with loans, arms, and the Yokosuka arsenal.

日本外史.note: Rai San’yō’s Unofficial History of Japan (1827), the stirring, imperial-centered history that did as much as any book to shape the loyalist feeling of the age. See ch12.

豊玉.note: Toshizō’s haiku pen-name, known only to his intimates; see ch19.

ch30.anchor: take supreme command of the Second Chōshū Expedition
ch30.note: The first expedition of 1864 (see ch27) had ended almost without fighting when Chōshū feigned submission and beheaded three of its elders. This second expedition, decreed in 1865, was another matter: the domain had swung back to its radicals and rearmed, and, as Shiba says, the shogunate had neither the money, the strength, nor a lawful pretext for it. The Shogun Iemochi came up to command it in person, fell ill at Osaka Castle, and died there in 1866 as the campaign went against him — the war that broke the Tokugawa. The account is historically accurate.

The uma-jirushi was the tall battle-standard that marked a commander’s place in the field. The golden fan had been the Tokugawa house’s device since Ieyasu; to see it carried into Kyōto was to see the shogun come in war-array, which is why the townsmen read it as a show of power restored.

ch30.anchor: the kind of sacred palanquin was different
ch30.note: The whole knot of the age in one image. Kondō and Itō both revere Kusunoki Masashige (see ch12), the model of the loyal vassal — but Kondō’s loyalty runs to the shogun and Itō’s to the Emperor, so the same hero is borne, as it were, in two different palanquins. Toshizō sees that men on the same side already march under opposed flags.

Napoleon III, emperor of the French, backed the shogunate through his minister Léon Roches with loans and arms and a scheme to remodel its forces on the French pattern (see ch27). Shiba’s aside looks ahead: this same emperor would be captured at Sedan in 1870 and his throne fall, so that the shogunate had staked its revival on a patron about to lose his own. The forward glance is accurate.

The secret compact by which Satsuma and Chōshū, until then at each other’s throats, agreed to make common cause against the shogunate. Brokered by the Tosa men Sakamoto Ryōma and Nakaoka Shintarō, it was sealed at Kyōto early in 1866, joining Saigō Takamori of Satsuma and Kido Takayoshi — the Katsura Kogorō of this book — of Chōshū. It is the hinge on which the Restoration turns, and, as Shiba stresses, the Shinsengumi, whose whole business was to police Kyōto for the shogunate, never suspected it. (Ryōma’s band, the Kaientai from 1867, was at this date still his Nagasaki company, the Kameyama Shachū; Shiba uses the later name.)

ch30.anchor: the French system of army organization
ch30.note: The corps was recast on Western lines: the old rank of jokin (roughly, officer) was dropped, and ten numbered units under captains put in its place, in imitation of the shogunate’s newly French-drilled infantry. The new post of staff officer (sanbō) given to Itō was, like Yamanami’s old ‘general secretary,’ a grand title with no troops under it. Toshizō kept the real command as vice-commander, and had drawn the whole roster to seat Itō’s faction where it could do least harm.

ch30.anchor: and I'd fain drink long (Chōshū) and deep.
ch30.note: A street lampoon (rakushu) built on two puns the parentheses gloss: kyatsu, ‘that fellow,’ for Aizu, the domain then holding Kyōto, and nagashi, ‘long,’ for Chōshū. The conceit is a wife-swap — cast off the Aizu spouse, take a better, and drink deep with Chōshū — and it measures how the capital’s sympathy had turned from the shogunate’s enforcers toward the beaten domain.

ch30.anchor: Hurrying toward home, the clouds of the Fifth Month.
ch30.note: The joke Okita catches: satsuki-gumo, ‘clouds of the Fifth Month,’ is a summer season-word (kigo), yet Toshizō writes it in the eleventh month, deep in autumn. He would sooner have the bright summer word than a lonely autumn one — a small window, as Okita sees, onto the homesick heart beneath the cold enforcer. Toshizō signs his verse Hōgyoku (see ch19).

Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official; here Grand Inspector (ōmetsuke), the office set to watch the daimyō. Late in 1865 he led an embassy to Hiroshima to interrogate Chōshū over the coming war, and Kondō, Itō, and two others rode in his train — Kondō under the borrowed name Kondō Kuranosuke. The mission is historical; the Chōshū side, as Shiba says, sent a stand-in envoy and never meant to treat.
